knownFor: Priest and master of Prague's university who preached in Czech at the Bethlehem Chapel from 1402 and would not condemn John Wyclif. He went to the Council of Constance under King Sigismund's safe-conduct, was arrested, refused to abjure what he said he had never taught, and was burned there on 6 July 1415. The lords and knights of Bohemia and Moravia then wrote to the council that he was a good, just and catholic man, and the lay cup he defended became the emblem of the Hussite and Bohemian Brethren movement.
datesNote: Born in 1369 by Palacký and Tomek, in 1373 by the oldest traditions, and between 1373 and 1375 by Count Lützow, who says the exact year cannot be affirmed and the day is quite uncertain; bachelor of divinity in 1394 and master of arts in 1396, priest probably in 1400, rector of the university in 1402 and again after the German masters left in 1409, all by Lützow; preacher at the Bethlehem Chapel from 1402; left Prague on 11 October 1414 and reached Constance on 3 November, by Lützow; arrested on 28 November 1414, by Peter of Mladoňovice; died on Saturday 6 July 1415, which Peter's text gives as the sixth day of July and Richental as the Saturday after St. Ulrich's day, though Palacký notes that Peter's manuscript reads the seventh day of July
placeNote: Husinec, near the small town of Prachatice in southern Bohemia, by Lützow; Prague, where he was a master of the university and preacher at the Bethlehem Chapel; Constance, where he was burned in a meadow outside the gate and his ashes were thrown into the Rhine
role: Priest, master of the university and preacher at the Bethlehem Chapel in Prague; martyr

keyWorks.title: De Ecclesia (the book on the Church)
keyWorks.about: written in exile between 1412 and 1414; it holds that the holy catholic church is the whole body of the predestinate, past, present and future, and that Christ alone is its head. David Schaff, its English translator, judges that Hus took paragraph after paragraph from Wyclif's own book on the Church, as Loserth showed. The council condemned the book at his sentence, and an edition was printed at Mainz in 1520

keyWorks.title: Letters
keyWorks.about: in Latin and Czech, with English by Herbert Workman and R. Martin Pope: among them his letter to the English master John Stokes about Wyclif's soul, his Czech letter to the Bethlehem congregation as he set out for Constance, and his letter from prison, after 18 June 1415, against the council's decree forbidding the cup to lay people

keyWorks.title: Czech works
keyWorks.about: Count Lützow names the Mirror of Sin and the Smaller Mirror, a series of expositions on the faith, the commandments and the Lord's Prayer from 1412, and a short work called the Daughter; he says scholars have added so many works, rightly or wrongly, that he mentions only a few

traces: On 2 September 1415 the barons, nobles and knights of Bohemia and Moravia, with 452 seals added, wrote to the council reproaching it for his condemnation and death; they said he was a good, just and catholic man, and vowed to defend the law of Christ and its preachers to the shedding of blood.

David Schaff writes that what Wyclif's Bible was to the small company of dissenters in England, Hus's book on the Church was to the large body of Bohemians, that Hussites sent a copy to Luther, and that Wyclif was not quoted by the Reformers, who knew him through Hus.

In 1520 Luther wrote in his Address to the Christian Nobility that Hus and Jerome of Prague were burned at Constance in violation of the papal, Christian and imperial oath and safe-conduct. He said he had no wish to make a saint or a martyr of Hus, as some Bohemians did, but owned that he was treated unjustly and that his books and doctrines were wrongfully condemned, and that he could find no error in him.

His burning turned a university movement into a national one. Its emblem was the chalice, its program was set out in the Four Articles of Prague in 1420, and in 1436 the Compacts of Basel gave it legal recognition.
remembered: 6 July, the day Hus was burned, is a public holiday in the Czech Republic.

Count Lützow reports a saying of Luther's, written when he had just begun to study Hus's works, that all had been Hussites without knowing it. The Library holds it only in Lützow's English, with no Latin or German.

Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini, later Pope Pius II, a hostile humanist writing about 1458, says that Hus and Jerome of Prague bore death with a steady mind, went to the fire as if invited to a feast, and sang hymns, and that no philosopher is said to have borne death so bravely. The Library's scan of this page is damaged and no second print is held, so the reading is uncertain.

uncertain: Birth. Palacký and Tomek give 6 July 1369, the oldest traditions 6 July 1373, and Lützow, after the latest research, a year between 1373 and 1375; he says the 6 July date rests on a fanciful likeness to the day of his death. Lützow says his parents were peasants of small means.

When he first spoke the wish that his soul be where Wyclif's is. At Constance, in Peter of Mladoňovice's record, Hus said he had said it twelve years before, when Wyclif's theological books were not yet in Bohemia and he knew only of his good life. Workman and Pope say, in a note, that he said it in a sermon before the synod in the presence of Archbishop Zbyněk, probably in June 1408. Hus's own reply to Stokes, as Workman and Pope give it, says he would not grant that Wyclif is a heretic but hopes he is among the saved; his written Latin reply confesses he said he wished to be in hope where Wyclif's soul is.

Wyclif's teaching on the bread. David Schaff says Hus was charged with holding that the bread and wine remain after the words of consecration, and that he declined to accept the university's decision of 1403. At Constance, in Peter's record, Hus answered that he had defended no error of Wyclif. Whether he held that teaching is contested.

The safe-conduct: when it was given. The letter is dated at Speyer on 18 October 1414, a week after Hus left Prague on 11 October, by Workman and Pope and Lützow. Workman and Pope say he set out without waiting for it, after Sigismund's promise dated at Rothenburg on 8 October, and Hus wrote that he had set out without safe-conduct. Peter says Sigismund promised the safe-conducts and afterwards sent them to meet him on the road. Sigismund told Hus at the hearing that he had given it before Hus left Prague. Some at the council said Hus's friends got it fifteen days after the arrest, and the Bohemian lords answered that it was shown and read to many on the day of the arrest. The exact sequence is contested.

The safe-conduct: what it covered. The Bohemian lords at Constance complained that Hus was held against the king's safe-conduct, and Hus wrote that in Bohemia he had been told to beware of it. Ulrich Richental, a Constance citizen hostile to Hus, writes that the king wished to help, thinking it a great shame if his safe-conduct were broken, but the learned told him that by no law could a heretic have a safe-conduct, and that when he heard their earnestness he let it be. Sigismund said at the hearing that he gave it so Hus could have a public hearing, and that some said he could not give it to a heretic. Workman and Pope judge that only the pope's safe-conduct could have protected him from the Inquisition, and that Sigismund's did not reach the church's courts. Luther judged that Hus was burned against the oath and safe-conduct. Cerretanus, a papal official, records that a knight who had brought Hus to Constance protested that the pope had given Hus a safe-conduct, which the pope denied. What it covered is contested.

The arrest. Peter of Mladoňovice, an eyewitness and Hus's partisan, dates it 28 November 1414, when the cardinals sent two bishops, the burgomaster and a knight for him; he says Hus told the bishops he would sooner choose death than deny a truth known to him from Scripture or otherwise. Peter also reports the rumor that Hus had been carried out of the city in a hay wagon and says it was false. Richental says Hus hid in a knight's hay wagon to get away, was found, and was then handed to the pope; he is hostile and inconsistent on the date. Cerretanus, a papal official, gives the council's reason: in his lodging at Constance Hus taught Wyclif's condemned doctrine to those who came to him, and when warned would not stop. Peter's date stands with Lützow and the editors. Workman and Pope, from Peter, say he was moved on 6 December to a dark cell hard by the latrines in the Dominican house.

The hearing of 7 June 1415. Peter, who was present, records that the king said he would defend no heretic and that if one stayed stubborn in his heresy he alone would light the fire and burn him; he also records that the council laughed at Hus and shook their heads.

The sentence of 6 July. The council's own text, in Mansi's volume, whose scan is damaged and has no second print here, says as far as it can be read that Hus had seduced the Christian people, most of all in Bohemia, was not a true preacher of Christ's gospel, was stubborn and past correction, and was to be deposed, degraded and left to the secular court. Peter says the sentence condemned his books, above all the book on the Church. Cardinal Fillastre's Gesta says he was convicted of many heresies and errors both by witnesses and by his book called On the Church, written in his own hand and acknowledged by him, and that in some points he made difficulty about abjuring because he said he had not said the things charged, but the contrary was proved. Peter and Fillastre each give why he would not abjure: Peter, that he feared to lie before God and to offend the truth and the many he had preached to; Fillastre, that he believed he would offend God and the saints and did not wish to scandalize the people to whom he had preached.

His death. Peter says he sang a prayer aloud until the wind blew the flame into his face, and then died praying silently with moving lips and head. Richental says that when the fire was lit he cried out very badly and was soon burned. Piccolomini, decades later and hostile, says they sang hymns and made no sound of a wretched mind. Count Lützow prints a contemporary Czech account of the death that Patera found; Patera doubts that its author was an eyewitness, though the writer says he was. The Library's scan of Piccolomini is damaged.

His confession. Richental says a priest offered to hear his confession if he would renounce his heresy, and Hus answered that there was no need, for he was no mortal sinner; he also says Hus wished to preach in German to the crowd and Duke Ludwig would not allow it. Peter says a priest on horseback said Hus should not be heard or given a confessor, as a heretic, and that Hus had confessed in prison to a monk and been absolved, as he wrote in his notes.

The ashes. Peter says the executioners broke the bones, burned the heart apart on a stick, threw his coat into the fire so that the Bohemians should not keep it for relics, and threw the ashes into the Rhine. Richental agrees that the ashes were carried into the Rhine.

Why he left Prague in 1412. Lützow says King Wenceslas begged him to leave for a short time and that Hus was also moved by the people's suffering under the interdict; he dates the departure probably to October 1412. Lützow says Hus disputed the papal indulgences publicly in June 1412, and that a decree of John XXIII granted a plenary indulgence to all who fought in or paid for the war against Ladislas, king of Naples; a second bull, Lützow says, ordered the Bethlehem Chapel, which it called a nest of heretics, destroyed and levelled to the ground. Hus defended his appeal to Christ at Constance, saying no appeal is safer than to Jesus Christ, who is not bent by a bribe or deceived by false witness.

The Bethlehem Chapel. Lützow dates its founding document, by John of Mühlheim, to 24 May 1391 and Hus's appointment as preacher to 1402. The bull of Gregory XII of 15 May 1408 confirms the foundation by the Prague citizen Kříž and the knight John of Mühlheim and says that, because no place in Prague was set aside for preaching, preachers in Czech were mostly forced to wander through houses and hidden corners.

Sigismund's titles. The safe-conduct is dated in his thirty-third year as king of Hungary and his fifth as king of the Romans, and it takes Hus under the protection of himself and the holy empire. Lützow says he was crowned emperor only in 1433, so he was king, not emperor, in 1414 and 1415.

The turn from a university quarrel into a national movement is an interpretation, widely accepted. The held primary witness for it is the lords' letter of 2 September 1415, which its heading puts at 452 seals; Hus's own letter on the cup is the bridge to the movement's emblem.

briefReferences: King Sigismund's safe-conduct, Speyer, 18 October 1414 (Palacký, Documenta): the king, the priest from Prague, the order to let him pass, stay, remain and return freely. His titles as king of Hungary and of the Romans, and Lützow's date for his crowning as emperor in 1433, give the opening's description of him.
Lützow and Schaff: Hus a master of the university; preacher at the Bethlehem Chapel from 1402. Gregory XII's bull of 1408: preachers in Czech wandering through houses and hidden corners.
Hus's reply to Stokes (Workman and Pope): he would not grant that Wyclif is a heretic and hoped he was among the saved.
Lützow and Schaff, 1403: the university forbids anyone to teach Wyclif's articles, and Hus protests. Lützow, 1410: the archbishop burns Wyclif's books and pronounces Hus excommunicated.

Lützow, 1412: the preaching against papal pardons, the heavier ban that forbids food, drink and speech with him, the city under a ban on Mass, sermons and burials, his appeal to Christ, and his leaving Prague in October.
Schaff: Christ alone the head of the Church, and the borrowing from Wyclif's book that Schaff credits to Loserth.

Cerretanus (Finke, volume 2): the council's reason for the arrest. Peter of Mladoňovice: most of the account of Constance, from an eyewitness who was in Hus's party. Richental: the learned who told the king that no heretic could hold a safe-conduct.

Peter's Relatio, 7 June 1415: the charge about Wyclif's soul, Hus's answer, the council's laughter, and the king's words about burning a stubborn heretic. Hus's letter from prison and Workman and Pope's note on the council's decree of 15 June 1415: the cup.

Peter's Relatio, 6 July 1415: the urging to abjure, the stripping of his priesthood, the paper hat painted with devils, the handing over, his last words, the song, the bones, the heart and the ashes in the Rhine; Richental on his crying out.

The lords' letter of 2 September 1415 (Palacký, Documenta): the seals, the verdict on Hus and the vow. World census, the Hussite and Bohemian Brethren movement: the cup as its emblem, the movement as a national one, and his story as its first voice.
Luther, 1520 (Address to the Christian Nobility): Hus burned against a sworn safe-conduct, and no wish to make a saint or a martyr of him.

quotationOriginals.modern: I do not know where John Wyclif's soul is. I hope that he is saved, and I fear that he may be damned. Yet in hope I would wish my soul to be where John Wyclif's soul is.
quotationOriginals.printed: Nescio, ubi est anima ipsius Joan. W.; spero, quod sit salvatus et timeo, ne sit damnatus; vellem tamen in spe, quod anima mea esset ibi, ubi est anima Joannis W.
quotationOriginals.work: Peter of Mladoňovice, Relatio, the hearing of 7 June 1415, in Latin, in Palacký's Documenta
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Peter's Latin shortens Wyclif's name to W. He records that Hus said he first spoke the words twelve years before; Workman and Pope place them in a sermon before the synod, probably in June 1408.

quotationOriginals.modern: God is my witness that I never taught or preached the things falsely charged to me, laid on me by false witnesses. The chief aim of my preaching, and of all my other acts and writings, was only to turn people from sin. I wrote, taught and preached the truth of the gospel from the words and teachings of the holy teachers. In that truth I will gladly die today.
quotationOriginals.printed: God is my witness that the evidence given against me is false. I have never thought nor preached save with the one intention of winning men, if possible, from their sins. In the truth of the gospel I have written, taught, and preached to-day I will gladly die.
quotationOriginals.work: Hus at the stake, 6 July 1415, in English, in Workman and Pope's narrative
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The modern words follow Peter of Mladoňovice's Latin in Palacký's Documenta, lines 17380-17388. Its scan has faults inside the passage (mnihi, i ntentione, wel, bomines, qp eccatis, qmraedicavi, 1 aetanter), and no second held print confirms the readings, so the Latin is not printed here. Workman and Pope's English is shorter and gives the words in the editors' own wording: it has the evidence against him false where the modern has the things falsely charged and laid on him by false witnesses; it has never thought nor preached where Peter's Latin has numquam docui nec praedicavi, never taught nor preached; and it has nothing for from the words and teachings of the holy teachers.

quotationOriginals.modern: Master John Hus was truly a good, just and catholic man. For many years he lived among us in our kingdom in a way worthy of praise, proven in his life, his conduct and his good name.
quotationOriginals.printed: quod ipse M. Joannes Hus fuit vir utique bonus, justus et catholicus, a multis annis in regno nostro vita, moribus et fama laudabiliter conversatus et comprobatus
